project_name: Bayesian optimization of likely negative candidates in imbalanced biological datasets
summary: High-throughput biological screens yield strongly class-imbalanced data because reliable negative examples are hard to obtain, which motivates positive-unlabeled (PU) learning\cite{ansari_learning_2023}. This team asked whether BO can choose the reliable negatives, treating the labeling of unlabeled peptides as the decision variable: at each iteration the current classifier scores the unlabeled pool, an acquisition function defined over the predicted class-probability distribution (expected improvement or an upper confidence bound) ranks the candidates, the top-ranked sequences are committed as negatives, and the classifier is retrained, with held-out AUC as the objective. On the hemolysis task (1826 positive, 7490 negative and 7295 unlabeled sequences), a classifier trained on the labeled data alone reached AUC 0.71 to 0.73. With a random-forest surrogate, the BO-selected negatives raised AUC to 0.78 within two iterations and held it through the seventh, after which AUC decayed to between 0.67 and 0.74 as the committed negative set grew, while accuracy rose monotonically from 0.02 to 0.40 over 20 iterations. A neural-ensemble variant reproduced the early gain (AUC 0.65 to 0.70) but cost minutes per retraining, limiting iterations. A second target, binding to the SHP-2 protein, was set up to compare EI, UCB and random selection but completed only one iteration within the event. (No video was submitted; summary prepared from the team's project page and repository notebooks.)
